source.text: וְ/עַתָּ֗ה שְׁב֨וּ נָ֥א בָ/זֶ֛ה גַּם אַתֶּ֖ם הַ/לָּ֑יְלָה וְ/אֵ֣דְעָ֔ה מַה יֹּסֵ֥ף יְהוָ֖ה דַּבֵּ֥ר עִמִּֽ/י־־׃

current_pob.text: Now please stay here tonight[a], you also, so that I may know what more Yahweh will say to me.

footnotes.text: Or 'what else the LORD will speak to me.'

records.context: Whole Numbers 22 read; focal unit 22:15–21, with 22:8–14 controlling the second delegation's repetition.
records.close_gloss: And now, remain please here, also you, tonight, and let me know what Yahweh will add to speak with me.
records.intended_improvement: Test whether the position of 'you also' obscures the new delegation's repetition and whether a more idiomatic clause adds information.
records.candidate: Now please stay here tonight, you too, so that I may know what more Yahweh will say to me.

rubric.meaning: Stay/remain, request particle, location, this night, additional delegation, volitional knowing and additional divine speech are conveyed.
rubric.omissions_additions: No material omission. 'Say to me' conveys the communication in דבר עמי. Do not add a wish to change God's mind or reward-seeking motive.
rubric.ambiguity: 'Will say' is an ordinary future in an embedded question, not a guarantee of permission. 'You also' attaches explicitly to the new visitors.
rubric.literary_function: Preserves the repetition of the overnight inquiry after the first delegation; the refusal in v12 and conditional permission in v20 remain distinct.
rubric.naturalness: The postposed 'you also' is slightly stiff. 'You too' is conversationally smoother but is not a demonstrated fidelity improvement.
rubric.consistency: Yahweh follows policy. Different 'lodge' in v8 and 'stay' here can preserve the different Hebrew verbs.

records.strongest_counterargument: The current placement of 'you also' interrupts the instruction; a reader may process the night twice before recognizing that the new delegation is being compared. 'You too' may improve oral flow.

confidence.semantic_rendering: high within this base and paragraph
confidence.preference: moderate: retain/tie, naturalness not tested on readers

records.source_choice: No source or vocalization change proposed.

ancillary_findings.problem: Marker [a] follows 'tonight' but note concerns the final divine-speech clause; note substitutes 'the LORD' against the current name policy.
ancillary_findings.candidate: Move [a] to the final clause and use: Or 'what else Yahweh will say to me.' Alternatively omit this nearly synonymous note after review.

records.reopen_when: A contextual reading establishes lost content, or a separate reader comparison shows the ordering materially hinders understanding.

source.text: וַ/יֹּ֤אמֶר דָּוִד֙ אֶל אֲבִישַׁ֔י עַתָּ֗ה יֵ֧רַֽע לָ֛/נוּ שֶׁ֥בַע בֶּן בִּכְרִ֖י מִן אַבְשָׁל֑וֹם אַ֠תָּה קַ֞ח אֶת עַבְדֵ֤י אֲדֹנֶ֨י/ךָ֙ וּ/רְדֹ֣ף אַחֲרָ֔י/ו פֶּן מָ֥צָא ל֛/וֹ עָרִ֥ים בְּצֻר֖וֹת וְ/הִצִּ֥יל עֵינֵֽ/נוּ־־־־־׃

current_pob.text: Then David said to Abishai[a], “Now Sheba son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. You, take your lord’s servants and pursue after him, lest he find fortified cities for himself and escape from our sight.”

footnotes.text: Hebrew literally, 'and deliver our eyes,' an idiom meaning 'escape from our sight' or 'elude us.'

records.context: Whole 2 Samuel 20 read; focal 20:4–7 (Amasa's delay, Abishai's commission), with 20:14–22 (fortified refuge and siege) as narrative payoff.
records.close_gloss: And David said to Abishai: Now Sheba son of Bichri will be worse for us than Absalom. You, take your lord's servants and pursue after him, lest he has found fortified cities for himself and has snatched away our eye [last clause uncertain].
records.intended_improvement: Test a local naturalness repair separately from the aspect of מצא and the disputed eye idiom.
records.candidate: Then David said to Abishai[a], “Now Sheba son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. You, take your lord’s servants and pursue him, lest he find fortified cities for himself and escape from our sight.”

rubric.meaning: Names, comparative threat, emphatic you, subordinate military servants, pursuit and fortified refuge are conveyed. 'Your lord' denotes David despite morphologically plural-looking אדניך. Final idiom and the perfect מצא need separate treatment.
rubric.omissions_additions: 'Pursue after him' double-marks the direction in English; 'pursue him' retains רדף אחריו. Literal sight-language is an interpretation of an unusual construction, not directly transparent equivalence.
rubric.ambiguity: The POB note declares a settled idiom; BDB records competing analyses. מצא is perfect in the pinned source, and fear that refuge may already have been secured differs from a purely prospective warning.
rubric.literary_function: The urgent pursuit follows Amasa's delay and anticipates the siege. This explains the practical escape reading but does not settle the precise eye metaphor or license emendation.
rubric.naturalness: 'Pursue him' is a defensible local readability gain. 'Lest' remains elevated but understandable. Neither this gain nor fluent idiom certifies the whole verse.
rubric.consistency: Retain servant/lord hierarchy. Existing YAML rationale says 'pursue him' while main text retains 'pursue after him'; prior review history is not fresh approval.

records.strongest_counterargument: Escape is a well-established contextual interpretation in BDB and fits the subsequent refuge; an English prospective apprehension clause may adequately convey the Hebrew perfect as a dreaded accomplished situation. Whole-verse abstention can be more conservative than needed for the two-word readability repair.
records.source_choice: Retain pinned מצא and והציל עיננו. BDB and NET discuss an imperfect emendation; no replacement Hebrew is adopted. Alternative analysis of the final verb/eye phrase is a source-interpretation question, not just smoother English.

ancillary_findings.kind: bounded naturalness recommendation, not whole-verse approval

ancillary_findings.candidate: Move note from Abishai to the final clause. Proposed note: Hebrew literally 'and snatch away our eye'; the expression is uncertain. 'Escape from our sight' is a contextual interpretation.
ancillary_findings.caution: The short note records uncertainty without promoting versional wording or an emendation.

records.reopen_when: Dedicated source-interpretation review of pen plus perfect and the unusual eye phrase, with exact lexicon/grammar and apparatus controls. A bounded readability edit can be evaluated separately without claiming full source approval.

source.text: גֶּֽבֶר חָכָ֥ם בַּ/ע֑וֹז וְ/אִֽישׁ דַּ֝֗עַת מְאַמֶּץ כֹּֽחַ־־־׃

current_pob.text: A wise man is strong[a], and a man of knowledge increases strength[b].

footnotes.text: The Hebrew is compact, literally, “A wise man in strength.”

records.context: Whole Proverbs 24 read; focal couplet 24:5–6, alongside 24:3–4. Verse 6 supplies the military application; nearby units are not forced into one paragraph.
records.close_gloss: A wise man [is] in strength, and a man of knowledge strengthens strength.
records.intended_improvement: Test whether specifying 'warrior' and supplying 'his' improves the sense enough to justify narrowing the present proverb.
records.candidate: A wise warrior is strong, and a man of knowledge increases his strength.

rubric.meaning: The first colon predicates strength of the wise man; the second uses a Piel participle with strength as object. POB conveys strengthening without changing it to a comparison of two men.
rubric.omissions_additions: The copula is a normal English supply. No possessive suffix is written on כח, but English 'his' could still be a defensible contextual clarification; absence of a suffix alone does not prove an unsupported addition.
rubric.ambiguity: 'Man' leaves the generic and military applications open; 'warrior' is well motivated by v6 but narrows the subject. 'Increases strength' leaves the possessor less explicit.
rubric.literary_function: Preserves two parallel nominal subjects and wisdom/knowledge, strength/strength correspondence; v6 explains the practical force through counsel in war.
rubric.naturalness: 'A man of knowledge' is somewhat formal but comprehensible; 'increases strength' is acceptable compressed proverbial English. No clear overall improvement demonstrated by candidate.
rubric.consistency: Retains source masculine personal nouns and generic application without inventing a gender rule. Doctrine requests context-sensitive fidelity; grammatical masculinity alone does not prove male-exclusive reference.

records.strongest_counterargument: Verse 6 concerns war and NET explicitly argues for the military sense of גבר; 'warrior' may make the literary linkage clearer. 'His strength' is more ordinary English and may articulate the natural referent without adding a new proposition.
records.source_choice: No source change. A 'better than a strong man' reading reported in modern version notes belongs to a versional/source-selection comparison; it is not claimed as a more fluent rendering of this pinned Hebrew.

ancillary_findings.problem: Canonical YAML already records an August 28 source audit addressing the possessive. This sample is preselected for this pass, but not a corpus-development held-out example.

records.reopen_when: A separate candidate/context judgment establishes whether military specification or possessive clarification improves understanding without unnecessary narrowing.

summary.limits: Not held-out from historical project development. One passage per stratum; no corpus-wide accuracy or improvement inference. Unflagged local WLC alignment is not a full apparatus finding.
